lesson.title: Lehnwörter I: Sofa, Radio, Klavier, Computer, Kino
lesson.subtitle: five words English handed over — and the German mouth that received them

hook.title: German Borrows Back
hook.content: For most of its history German lent English words; this lesson is the border crossing in the other direction — and every word that crosses, German says with its own mouth. der Computer is an English loan: English built it on Latin computare, 'to reckon up', and German bought the finished English word — the newest purchase on your shelf. das Klavier came through French clavier, from Latin clavis, 'key' — the piano is literally a key-board, and English kept the same key-root in clavichord (and in clavicle, the shoulder's 'little key'). das Kino is a German shortening of Kinematograph — Greek kinēma, 'movement' — and cinema is the same Greek word English uses. das Radio hides Latin radius, 'ray' — the ray that carries the signal. das Sofa walked the longest road: Arabic ṣuffa, a cushioned bench, that both languages borrowed whole. German writes them almost as English does — then pronounces them as if it had invented them: KEE-no, kla-VEER.

footnotes.title: Why So Much das?
footnotes.content: Four of the five arrive as das — das Sofa, das Radio, das Kino, das Klavier; only der Computer is der. Borrowed things tend to start neuter in German and earn their article over time. The gender is German's decision, not the donor's.

pattern.title: Same Letters, German Mouth
pattern.content: The frames are everyday German: Das Auto hat ein Radio. Ich sitze auf dem Sofa. Der Computer ist neu. Im Kino sehen wir einen Film — in + dem, German's where-frame, doing for Kino what at does for cinema. What German did not change: the spellings are nearly the English ones. What it did change: the mouth — final -o stays long (Kino, Radio), the W in Klavier is the V-sound, and the stress lands where German wants it: KEE-no, kla-VEER.
pattern.linguist_note: A loanword's stress tells you when it arrived. Kino, Sofa and Radio took German's comfortable first-syllable beat; Klavier kept its French final stress — kla-VIER — a little Paris still audible inside German.

exercises.prompt: The borrowed objects in their natural frames — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The dog sits on the sofa
matching_pairs.german: Der Hund sitzt auf dem Sofa

matching_pairs.english: The piano is big and heavy
matching_pairs.german: Das Klavier ist groß und schwer

matching_pairs.english: At the cinema we watch a film
matching_pairs.german: Im Kino sehen wir einen Film

exercises.target_answer: Der Hund sitzt auf dem Sofa, Das Auto hat ein Radio, Der Computer ist neu, Das Klavier ist groß und schwer, Im Kino sehen wir einen Film
exercises.explanation: Five loanwords in five German frames: auf dem Sofa, im Kino, hat ein Radio. The words are international; the grammar around them is pure German.

exercises.prompt: das Klavier names which instrument in German?
exercises.explanation: Klavier came through French clavier from Latin clavis, 'key' — the black-and-white keys are the whole word. English named the clavichord with that same Latin key, but German's Klavier is the everyday piano.

exercises.prompt: Which neuter singular article does German assign to international loanwords like Sofa, Radio, Kino, and Klavier?
exercises.meaning: das Sofa, das Radio, das Kino, das Klavier — the neuter default
exercises.explanation: Borrowed things tend to start neuter: das Sofa, das Radio, das Kino, das Klavier. Only der Computer breaks the pattern. German assigns the gender; the donor language has no vote.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the where-frame: 'The cinema is in the city'
exercises.target_answer: Das Kino ist in der Stadt
exercises.meaning: The cinema is in the city
exercises.explanation: Where-frames take in + dative: in der Stadt, im Haus, im Auto. das Kino stays das even as the subject — the frame around it is what changes.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The house has a computer and a radio'
exercises.target_answer: Das Haus hat einen Computer und ein Radio
exercises.meaning: The house has a computer and a radio
exercises.explanation: Two accusatives, two endings: der Computer becomes einen Computer in the accusative, das Radio stays ein Radio. The loanwords inflect exactly like the native nouns — borrowing changes the vocabulary, never the grammar.

summary.outcome: Recognize the five loans, use them in German frames — im Kino, auf dem Sofa — and say them German-style: KEE-no, kla-VEER.

use_example.german: Das Klavier ist groß und schwer — im Kino sehen wir einen Film.
use_example.english: The piano is big and heavy — at the cinema we watch a film.

summary.takeaway: Sofa, Radio, Klavier, Computer, Kino — Arabic, Latin and Greek roots, with Computer the English-built one — that German writes like English and says like German; four of the five are das.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Hotel, Taxi, Bus, Theater, Hobby — the travel-and-leisure layer.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Lehnwörter I: Sofa, Radio, Klavier, Computer, Kino (The house has a computer and a radio):
twist.target_answer: Das Haus hat einen Computer und ein Radio
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Das Haus hat einen Computer und ein Radio" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Lehnwörter I: Sofa, Radio, Klavier, Computer, Kino without relying on short-term echo.

sofa.context_translation: The sofa is in the living room.
sofa.etymology_derivation: From French sofa, ultimately Arabic ṣuffa — the same loan route as English sofa. [wiktionary]

radio.context_translation: We listen to the radio in the car.
radio.etymology_derivation: Borrowed about 1920 from English radio, short for radiotelegraphy - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

klavier.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French clavier, from Latin clavis 'key' — a Romance loan. [wiktionary]

computer.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English computer - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

kino.context_translation: We are going to the cinema.
kino.etymology_derivation: Clipping of Kinematograph, the Greek-rooted invention name — a shared international loan. [wiktionary]

auto.etymology_derivation: Short for Automobil — the same Greek autos ('self') loan as English auto, clipped German-style. [wiktionary]

hund.context_phrase: Der Hund schläft auf dem Sofa.
hund.context_translation: The dog sleeps on the sofa.
hund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaz — cognate with English hound, the same ancient dog-word. [wiktionary]

sitzen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
sitzen.context_translation: We are sitting in the café.

film.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English film — a direct English loan into German. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

neu.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German niuwe, Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, the exact twin of English new; both go back to the same Indo-European root. [wiktionary]

schwer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *swēraz 'heavy, grave'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

stadt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *stadiz — the twin of stead (homestead, instead); final d devoiced to [t]. [wiktionary]

ende.context_phrase: Am Ende des Films weine ich immer.
ende.context_translation: At the end of the film I always cry.
ende.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *andijaz — the same root as English end. [wiktionary]

lehren.etymology_derivation: The causative of the lore root (*laizō): German splits the learn family into lernen (learn) and lehren (teach); the page documents archaic English lear as cognate and glosses the root noun as lore. [wiktionary]
